name: transmediale
funding: Annual festival (2026) funded since 2004 by the Kulturstiftung des Bundes. Berlin Senate, bpb and Creative Europe funding was listed for 2020 to 2021.
watch: Its 2026 partner programmes include the Schering Stiftung and HAU.
records_note: Its old partner page shows funder logos and its about page names two funders.
affiliations_note: Listed among the current partners of the European Media Art Platform (EMAP). Member of European Media Art Platform. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: Annual Berlin festival for art and digital culture. The 2026 edition, the 39th, ran from 28 January to 1 February 2026 at silent green Kulturquartier (Gerichtstraße 35) and CANK (Karl-Marx-Straße 95), curated by Neema Githere and Juan Pablo García Sossa (e-flux).

Founded in 1988 as VideoFilmFest, a side programme of the Berlinale's International Forum of New Cinema, initiated by Hartmut Horst and Micky Kwella. Renamed VideoFest in 1989, transmedia in 1997 and transmediale in 1998 (Wikipedia).

Kulturprojekte Berlin organised the festival until 2020. Since then the independent association transmediale e.V. has organised and managed it (Wikipedia; Kulturprojekte Berlin). The association's office is at silent green, Gerichtstraße 35 (Wikipedia).
Artistic directors: Andreas Broeckmann (2001 to 2007), Stephen Kovats (from 2007), Kristoffer Gansing (from 2012) and Nóra Ó Murchú (from 2021, departure announced in July 2024) (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: transmediale: mainly public: the German Federal Cultural Foundation (Kulturstiftung des Bundes)
funding: The festival has been funded as a "cultural institution of excellence" by the Kulturstiftung des Bundes since 2004 (transmediale website; Kulturstiftung des Bundes project page for transmediale 2021 to 2022). Kulturprojekte Berlin says the federal government has funded it as a flagship project since 2004.

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: 2025: an open letter by !Mediengruppe Bitnik, Aram Bartholl, Constant Dullaart and Danja Vasiliev, sent to transmediale e.V. (Filippo Gianetta and Magdalena Ritter) and its advisory board on 1 February 2025 and forwarded to the nettime list by Andreas Broeckmann on 2 February 2025. It asked the leadership to make transparent the basis of its decisions, said Ó Murchú's departure in summer 2024 was "not transparently communicated", and objected to a 10-month lead-curator post with the exhibition element removed (nettime).

press.overall: One essay on the festival's 2024 statement and Berlin's political climate, and one open letter on the 2025 leadership change and cancelled exhibition.

items.title: Adina Glickstein, "The Highs and Lows of transmediale 2024" (14 February 2024)
points: Frames the festival as shaped by Berlin's political climate and the war in Gaza, including a Berlin Senate clause requiring state-funded artists to pledge opposition to antisemitism, which she argues conflated antisemitism with anti-Zionism. The Senate dropped the clause in January 2024.

Reads the festival's statement, which condemned the clause and called for "safeguarding a free and respectful space for dialogue, openness and exchange", as a hedged appeal, noting that the statement says the festival depends on state funding.

Says the #StrikeGermany boycott led to withdrawals, and that the panel "Anti-Colonial Tech through Resistance and Discomforts" was cancelled on the day; its panelists later said they were told they "could not be explicit about a certain solidarity".

items.title: Andreas Broeckmann forwarding an open letter to transmediale, "Re: <nettime> Transmedialle intel?" (2 February 2025)
points: Argues that a lead-curator post on a 10-month contract (April 2025 to February 2026) leaves little room for a multi-year vision and asks why no artistic director is being hired.
Argues that the call, which removes the exhibition element, constrains the new post. In the forwarded thread, Ursula Damm writes that the festival has become a "media-theoretical conference".
Addressed to transmediale e.V. (Filippo Gianetta and Magdalena Ritter) and the advisory board.

wider_context: 2024 withdrawals: the #StrikeGermany boycott, with over 1,600 signatories, asked artists to withdraw from publicly funded German cultural institutions and events "such as transmediale". Artists including Avril Corroon withdrew from transmediale 2024. The festival said "several artists and a curator" had withdrawn (Spike Art Magazine, Adina Glickstein, 14 February 2024). The boycott opposed the Berlin Senate clause and German state policy on the war in Gaza, not transmediale alone; the festival's own 19 January statement condemned the clause.

The Berlin Senate's clause: culture senator Joe Chialo introduced it on 21 December 2023, requiring funding recipients to oppose antisemitism as defined by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance. Almost 6,000 cultural workers and artists signed an open letter against it, and the Senate dropped it about a month later, in January 2024 (The Art Newspaper, Catherine Hickley, 22 January 2024).
details.bottom_line: The money behind transmediale is German public arts funding: the Kulturstiftung des Bundes has funded it as a cultural institution of excellence since 2004. In 2025 an open letter criticised the festival's leadership change and the removed exhibition element; the 2024 artist withdrawals were a boycott of German state-funded institutions over the Berlin Senate clause.

name: Acropolis Museum
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts.
watch: The museum built to house the finds from the Acropolis and its slopes, with a Parthenon Gallery that shows the frieze, metopes and pediments; Greece wants the Parthenon sculptures held by the British Museum reunified here. To Vima (23 September 2026) and iefimerida (24 September 2026) relayed a Daily Telegraph report that talks between Greece and the British Museum, begun in 2021, have stalled over ownership, while the British Museum says discussions remain constructive.

overview: The Acropolis Museum is at 15 Dionysiou Areopagitou in Athens; its exhibition areas run over three levels above an archaeological excavation of an ancient Athenian neighbourhood, visible through glass floors (Greek National Tourism Organisation).
It was created to house the finds from the Sacred Rock of the Acropolis and its slopes (Greek National Tourism Organisation).

The Gallery of the Acropolis Slopes shows finds from the sanctuaries and settlement on the hillside; the Archaic Acropolis Gallery shows sculptures from the early temples and votive offerings such as the Korai and the horsemen; the Parthenon Gallery on the third level shows the frieze of the Panathenaic procession, the metopes and the two pediments; sculptures of the Propylaea, the Temple of Athena Nike and the Erechtheion are on the first level (Greek National Tourism Organisation).
About 60% of the surviving sculptural material of the Parthenon is in Athens (iefimerida, 24 September 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Acropolis Museum: funding not stated on the pages read
funding: No reporting found, in the pages read, of the museum's budget, its state funding or its ticket income.

red_flags.heading: Contested holdings: the Parthenon sculptures in London
points: The Daily Telegraph reported that talks between Greece and the British Museum, which began in 2021, have stalled over ownership and over whether the sculptures could come to Athens on a long-term loan; no talks are under way (To Vima, 23 September 2026; iefimerida, 24 September 2026).

British law allows only a loan, which would require Greece to recognise the British Museum's ownership, a condition Athens refuses; a 'hybrid deal' exchanging long-term returns for rotating loans of other Greek objects also fell through (iefimerida, 24 September 2026).

British Museum chairman George Osborne called the sculptures the institution's 'most intractable problem' in December 2025; Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis told UNESCO's director-general on 11 September that reunification remains a national priority (To Vima; iefimerida).
The British Museum says discussions over a 'new Parthenon Partnership' remain 'constructive and ongoing' (iefimerida, 24 September 2026).

details.bottom_line: Who pays for the museum is not on the pages read, so this record cannot say. What is contested is not in the building: the Parthenon sculptures in London, which Greece wants shown here. Watch whether talks with the British Museum resume.

name: National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA)
funding: Government of India. A subordinate office of the Ministry of Culture, founded in 1954, with branches in Mumbai and Bengaluru.
watch: In 2000 the Culture Ministry ordered a painting pulled and all the artists withdrew. In 2019 members cut off Amol Palekar's criticism of the ministry.
records_note: It posts nothing itself; its parent Ministry of Culture publishes annual reports from 2014-15 to 2023-24, with no sponsor list or advisory board named.
affiliations_note: NGMA runs regional centres in Mumbai and Bengaluru and opened an NGMA Kolkata in 2025.

overview: India's national museum of modern art, at Jaipur House by India Gate in the Central Hexagon at the end of Rajpath, New Delhi.

Established on 29 March 1954 by the Government of India. Inaugurated by Vice-President S. Radhakrishnan with Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru present. Hermann Goetz, a German art historian, was its first curator (Wikipedia).
Housed in Jaipur House, a former residence of the Maharaja of Jaipur, a butterfly-shaped building with a central dome built in 1936 and designed by Sir Arthur Blomfield (Wikipedia).
About 17,000 works by roughly 2,000 artists, mainly Indian, with about 12,000 square metres of exhibition space in Delhi and branches in Mumbai and Bangalore (Wikipedia).
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 11am to 6:30pm. Entry is 20 rupees for Indian citizens aged 18 and over and 500 rupees for foreign nationals (Tour My India, a travel listing, not the gallery).
details.funding_verdict: National Gallery of Modern Art: public: Government of India, Ministry of Culture
funding: Run by the Government of India under the Ministry of Culture (Wikipedia); the Ministry told the press in 2019 that the gallery's advisory committees in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Delhi had not been dissolved and that their terms had recently ended (Tribune, PTI).

red_flags.heading: Ministry control of what is shown
points: September 2000: at the exhibition "CombineVoice for the New Century", Culture Ministry Secretary P. V. Vaidynatha Ayyar ordered director Mukta Nidhi Samnotra to remove Surendran Nair's painting of a nude Icarus on the Ashoka Pillar, on the ground that it treated the national emblem irreverently. Samnotra agreed; all 25 artists withdrew their works in protest (The File Room archive, an anti-censorship project; ArtsJournal, citing the BBC, 5 September 2000).

February 2019: at the Mumbai branch, the actor-director Amol Palekar criticised the Ministry for scrapping the branch advisory committees and was interrupted by some NGMA members at an exhibition opening (Tribune, 11 February 2019). Director General Adwaita Gadanayak said the committees were not dissolved but their terms had ended, and that their earlier recommendations would be honoured (Latestly, 11 February 2019). The Ministry said the same (Tribune).

May 2023: the Delhi gallery hosted "Jan Shakthi: A Collective Power", curated by Alka Pandey, with themes from Narendra Modi's radio broadcast "Mann Ki Baat"; South First called it "reportedly pro-government" (South First, 13 July 2023).

press.overall: The objections found are to ministry control of programming, and none comes from a dedicated art outlet.

items.title: Gautam Benegal, "No Podium for Palekar: When art is attacked, it's the people who lose" (2019)
points: Argues that a policy, in force since October 2018, giving the Ministry of Culture control over NGMA exhibitions threatens artistic freedom; before it, local artists' committees chose the Mumbai and Bangalore shows.
Names Palekar, Suhas Bahulkar, Jesal Thacker and NGMA Mumbai director Anita Rupavataram; also questions the Delhi NGMA's January 2019 auction of gifts given to Modi.
A news site, not an art outlet.

items.title: Sreerag PS, "Artists stand in solidarity with museum employee fired for criticising pro-government art exhibition" (2023)
points: Reports that Sandip K Luis lost his contract at the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art after a 15 May 2023 post criticising the artists behind "Jan Shakthi" at NGMA Delhi.
Criticises the artists and the Kiran Nadar Museum; does not itself criticise NGMA.

items.title: Douglas McLennan, post citing the BBC (2000)
points: Reports that a painting of a small nude figure was removed from a Delhi exhibition and all 25 artists withdrew.
Does not name NGMA.

wider_context: DailyO places the 2019 episode within pressure on Indian artists by Hindutva groups, citing the arrest of the Baroda art student Chandramohan more than 10 years earlier and the 8 December 2016 attack on the Jaipur Art Summit.
NGMA is the state's own gallery, so the Ministry's decisions on its programme are the ones DailyO criticises.
details.bottom_line: The money behind NGMA is the Government of India's, with no sponsors found. The weak points are documented ministry orders over what is shown (the 2000 removal) and complaints about a state-friendly programme in 2019 and 2023. Watch for published budgets and for who curates the gallery's shows.

name: Israel Philharmonic Orchestra
funding: The pages read did not state the orchestra's funding. The New Arab (7 November 2025) did not mention funding.
watch: An orchestra whose concert at the Paris Philharmonie on 6 November 2025 was interrupted by protesters with flares; four people were detained, and the musicians returned and finished the concert (The New Arab, 7 November 2025).
why_flagged: The New Arab, 7 November 2025, reported that protesters set off flares during the orchestra's Paris concert on 6 November 2025 and four people were detained.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A symphony orchestra based in Tel Aviv; its concert hall in the pages read was not confirmed, and the coordinates are for Heichal HaTarbut.
The pages read gave no founding date.
What is there: an orchestra touring internationally; no repertoire or season was read.
Archive: the pages read did not describe one.
details.funding_verdict: Israel Philharmonic Orchestra: funding not found in the pages read.
funding: No reporting found, in the pages read, of Ministry of Culture grants, donors or sponsors.

red_flags.heading: Protest at a tour concert
points: On 6 November 2025 protesters set off flares twice during the orchestra's concert at the Paris Philharmonie, the musicians left the stage, and audience members lunged at protesters in video; four people were detained (The New Arab, 7 November 2025).
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez wrote on X that nothing can justify the disruptions (The New Arab, 7 November 2025).

details.bottom_line: Funding is not in the pages read. The documented controversy is the 2025 protest at a Paris tour concert.

name: Tower of David Museum
funding: The Jewish Chronicle (1 June 2023) said the refurbishment was supported in part by Dame Vivien Duffield and the Clore Israel Foundation, put the refurbishment at $50 million in its text, and said the museum is over 84 per cent self-funded (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023).
watch: Jerusalem's city museum in the Old City, reopened in June 2023 after a renewal backed by Dame Vivien Duffield and the Clore Israel Foundation. It is over 84 per cent self-funded per the Jewish Chronicle.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: The city museum of Jerusalem in the Old City.
Initiated in 1989 by then mayor Teddy Kollek; the renewed museum was unveiled in the week of 1 June 2023 (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023).

What is there: the Illes model of Jerusalem made for the 1873 Vienna World Fair, found in a Geneva University Library attic in 1984; newly found Hasmonean-period towers and a Crusader tunnel (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023).
Archive: the renovation drew on the 1930s excavation diary and photographs of archaeologist Cedric Norman Johns (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023). Director and chief conservator is Eilat Lieber.
details.funding_verdict: Tower of David Museum: mostly self-funded, plus one large philanthropic gift.
funding: Dame Vivien Duffield and the Clore Israel Foundation supported the creation in 1989 and the renovation, which the article put at a $50 million refurbishment while its headline said 40 million; no amount per donor given (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023).

red_flags.heading: Rockefeller Museum tours, not the Tower
points: Times of Israel reported that a December 2023 document discussed selling or leasing the Rockefeller Museum for a hotel; Tower of David director Eilat Lieber said the museum's interest in the Rockefeller is historical and cultural. That row concerns the Rockefeller, not the Tower of David Museum.

details.bottom_line: Largely earned income, with a major gift from the Clore Israel Foundation. No controversy at the Tower itself was read.

records_note: The pages read did not link published accounts.

What is there: a collection section on Costantino Nivola (museum website). The pages read gave no object count.
The site names a Fondazione section and a foundation contact; the pages read did not state its role.

It opened in 2010 in a reconstruction of the red brick Mitsubishi Ichigokan designed by Josiah Conder and first built in 1894 (Tokyo Art Beat).
What is there: the collection focuses on late 19th-century Western art, with Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Odilon Redon and Felix Vallotton named; the page gives no object count (Tokyo Art Beat).
The pages read do not describe a library or archive.

name: National Visual Arts Gallery
funding: Owned by the Government of Malaysia and run by the National Visual Art Development Board, a statutory body under the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture. Most exhibitions are free.
watch: In February 2020 it removed four works from Ahmad Fuad Osman's retrospective. Nearly 400 artists and 55 collectors petitioned; a deputy minister sought their return.
records_note: Annual reports for 2023 and 2024 are posted but password protected. The board is listed as an image, and six former sponsors are named, undated.

overview: National art museum on Jalan Temerloh, off Jalan Tun Razak, on the northern edge of central Kuala Lumpur, next to Istana Budaya (Wikipedia). A city guide puts it 10 to 15 minutes by car from KLCC (kualalumpurcity.my).
The first exhibition was held in August 1958, opened by Tunku Abdul Rahman. Its first home was at 109 Jalan Ampang (Wikipedia).
Earlier names: Balai Seni Lukis Negara (1958 to 1977 and 1981 to 2010), Muzium Seni Negara (1978 to 1980), Balai Seni Visual Negara (2011 to 2017) (Wikipedia).

Own building built by YTL Corporation from 1996 to 1998, opened 27 September 2000. Architects MAA Akitek and Dato' Mir Shahriman. Cost MYR 40 million on a 5.67 acre site. Galleries flank a circular ramp (Wikipedia).
Visiting: open daily 9am to 5pm, free for most exhibitions, some special exhibitions need a ticket. On-site parking (kualalumpurcity.my).
details.funding_verdict: National Visual Arts Gallery: mainly public: Government of Malaysia
funding: The Government of Malaysia owns the gallery and a statutory board under the ministry runs it (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Removal of four works from a state gallery show, February 2020
points: The gallery, operated by the National Visual Art Development Board, a statutory body under the Ministry of Tourism, Art and Culture (Wikipedia), pulled four works on 4 February 2020 (The Edge) from Ahmad Fuad Osman's retrospective "At the End of the Day Even Art is Not Important (1990 to 2019)", which opened on 29 October 2019. Osman said on 10 February 2020 they were taken down without his consent (ArtsEquator, Kathy Rowland).

Director General Amerruddin Ahmad said the gallery could remove works touching the "dignity of any individual, religion, politics, race, culture and country", and that "an exhibition is a process and not a final product" (The Edge).

ArtsEquator reported (15 February 2020) that the gallery insisted "Imitating the Mountain" (2004) stay removed as obscene, although it had approved it and shown it for three months. The Edge described it as a painting that depicts nudity and said the artist rejected a plan to restore only three works.

Unverified: Osman's statement alleged the gallery acted at the behest of an unnamed member of its board of directors (ArtsEquator, 11 February 2020). The Edge reported the removal followed a board member's complaint that the works were "political and obscene".

Outcome: all four works were reinstated and the show was extended to 29 February 2020 (The Edge). The Edge reported that the directive to reinstate came from the ministry and Deputy Prime Minister Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, not the gallery.

red_flags.heading: Protest by artists and collectors
points: 55 private collectors signed a petition saying they would stop lending works unless the pieces were reinstated; it said the removal "relates to accountability and transparency in the management of exhibitions in publicly funded art museums" (ArtsEquator, 15 February 2020).
A public petition for Osman received 396 signatures (The Edge); ArtsEquator said close to 400 within two days.

Deputy Minister Muhammad Bakhtiar Wan Chik wrote to the gallery in a personal capacity, calling the show "international class" and urging respect for freedom of expression (The Edge); ArtsEquator reported he asked it to return the works and apologise to Osman.

press.overall: Criticism comes from one art outlet, ArtsEquator, and is aimed at the gallery's handling of the 2020 removal.

items.title: Kathy Rowland, "Arts censorship: At the end of the day, this is not new" (2020)
points: Calls the removal "a tragedy all of Balai's own making" and argues the gallery sacrificed the artist's rights.
Places it in a pattern of removals in 1999, 2013 and 2017.
Calls the director's "a process, and not a final product" line chilling, since it implies any work entering the gallery ceases to be a final product as its creator deems it.

items.title: Kathy Rowland, "Leading art collectors put pressure on Balai Seni Visual Negara" (2020)
points: Reports the collectors' petition and the artists' petition, and that the gallery was to reinstate only three of four works at the time of writing.

details.bottom_line: The gallery is a state body, so the money behind it is public rather than corporate. The weak point is editorial control: in February 2020 it removed four works and reversed only after artists, collectors and a deputy minister objected. Watch for a published budget or sponsor list.

name: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean (ICAIO)
funding: Founded in 2015 by Salim Currimjee, a painter, architect and collector (Lonely Planet France).
watch: Exhibitions change each quarter, showing Mauritian, Indian and South African artists, at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis.
records_note: The institute's domain now redirects to an unrelated site and its archived pages hold no readable text, so nothing could be checked.

overview: Gallery at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis, in a historic stone building (Lonely Planet France).
Boston College describes it as "an independent, nonprofit foundation that is a platform for art education and public art programming in Mauritius" (Boston College news).

Its stated aim is "faire de Maurice le carrefour artistique et culturel de l'océan Indien", in Lonely Planet's French text (translation: to make Mauritius the artistic and cultural crossroads of the Indian Ocean).

Exhibitions change every quarter and show Mauritian, Indian and South African artists (Lonely Planet France). In 2020 it held the solo exhibition "Walk of Life" by the artist Portia Zvavahera (Kettle's Yard).
Currimjee also co-curated "Indian Ocean Current: Six Artistic Narratives" at the McMullen Museum of Art, Boston College, in 2020 (Boston College news).
Visiting: open Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 17:00 (Lonely Planet France).
details.funding_verdict: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean: nonprofit foundation: set up by Salim Currimjee
funding: Founder: Currimjee established the institute in 2015 (Boston College news, Lonely Planet France).
details.bottom_line: The institute is a nonprofit foundation founded in 2015 by the painter, architect and collector Salim Currimjee.
